solutionSource.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

indicatorNotes.unfinished: the temple loses its final letter, so it never gets finished

blocks.note: PARTHENON, the Athens temple, without its last N
the first book of the Bible

annotation.surface: A note on a temple building that never got finished and the book that reproduces it.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Reproduction' looks like a copy of the book; it is the biological sense.
annotation.definitionFit: Parthenogenesis is reproduction from an unfertilised egg, as in some insects and plants.

entries.clue: Ask for money in God’s name? (9)

blocks.note: the Greek god of the wild
a handle is a name or title

annotation.surface: Someone begging for cash in the name of God, like a street preacher with a collecting tin.
annotation.walkthrough: The phrase 'in God's name' reads as an oath, but it is Pan's handle.
annotation.definitionFit: To panhandle is to beg in the street, originally American slang.

blocks.note: the surface wants a playground game of twirling; the setter means spinning a revolver's cylinder
not a circle but a single bullet, the one live round in the chamber

annotation.surface: A children's game where you spin round and round until dizzy.
annotation.walkthrough: The 'round' is a bullet: in Russian roulette you spin a revolver's cylinder holding one round.
annotation.definitionFit: Russian roulette is a deadly game of spinning a revolver with one live round and firing at yourself.

blocks.note: a verb: to curve your spine and shoulders forward

annotation.surface: A strange sensation creeping around your back.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Round' is a verb here, not a preposition.
annotation.definitionFit: Two plain senses: a noun for an intuition, and a verb for curling the shoulders forward.

blocks.note: flowers that are out are blooming

annotation.surface: The outer rim of a bunch of flowers in full bloom.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Edge' is a verb, to win narrowly, and the bouquet is a wine's, not a florist's.
annotation.definitionFit: To nose out a rival is to edge past them by a small margin.

indicatorNotes.over: turned over, so the letters run backwards in this down answer

blocks.note: a ram butts, so it is a butter

annotation.surface: Butter smeared across the cover of a book.
annotation.walkthrough: Butter and spread look like kitchen synonyms; the butter is an animal that butts.
annotation.definitionFit: A grammar is a book setting out the rules of a language.

entries.clue: Men declared success at snooker club (9)

indicatorNotes.declared: said out loud, so we want the sound of the word

annotation.surface: Players announce a winning shot at their snooker hall.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Snooker club' reads as one place; the club is the definition, split off from the snooker.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: a club open late for drinking and dancing is a nightspot.

blocks.note: the surface wants actors; the setter means musicians
not bowing to applause but picking up the bows of violins, violas and cellos

annotation.surface: Actors taking their curtain call at the end of a show.
annotation.walkthrough: Taking bows sounds like the curtain call; these players take up bows to play violins and cellos.
annotation.definitionFit: Definition by description: an ensemble of violins, violas, cellos and basses, all played with bows.

indicatorNotes.filling: the answer fills the inside of the words that follow

blocks.note: the answer sits inside, straddling the two words, without the first three letters and the last one

annotation.surface: Soil or rubble used to cover and fill in an old rubbish tip.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Ground cover' sounds like landfill topping; it is a plant.
annotation.definitionFit: Sedum, or stonecrop, is a low succulent often planted as ground cover.

annotation.surface: A claim that November is a new month in the calendar.
annotation.walkthrough: November looks like the month in question; it is only the letter N.
annotation.definitionFit: Nisan is a spring month of the Jewish calendar.

entries.clue: Was lurcher good separating deer and wild deer? (9)

annotation.definitionNote: a lurcher here is one who lurches, so 'was lurcher' means lurched

indicatorNotes.separating: G sits between the two deer
indicatorNotes.wild: the second deer runs wild, its letters jumbled

annotation.surface: Did the lurcher, a hunting dog, get between the deer as they scattered?
annotation.walkthrough: A lurcher is a British crossbred hunting dog, ideal for deer; here it is simply someone who lurches.
annotation.definitionFit: To stagger is to lurch unsteadily.

entries.clue: After this, picked up a hanky? (7)

annotation.definition: After this, picked up a hanky?

indicatorNotes.picked up: heard, so we want the sound

blocks.note: a tissue is a paper hanky

annotation.surface: After a sneeze, someone grabs a hanky.
annotation.walkthrough: The whole clue is the scene: you reach for a tissue after an atishoo, and the tissue said out loud is the sneeze.
annotation.definitionFit: Atishoo is the British written sound of a sneeze, which is what sends you for a hanky.

entries.clue: Short note about theatre award for Broadway? (7)

indicatorNotes.Short: the memo is cut short by its last letter

blocks.note: the Tony Awards for Broadway theatre

annotation.surface: A brief memo about a Tony Award won by a Broadway show.
annotation.walkthrough: The Tony and Broadway look like one theatre story; Broadway is only the example of a metonym.
annotation.definitionFit: Broadway stands for the whole New York theatre industry, which makes it a metonym.

indicatorNotes.jockeys: to jockey is to jostle about, moving the letters

annotation.surface: The riders at a racecourse are fearless.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Jockeys' reads as the riders; it is the verb that shuffles the letters. Doncaster is a Yorkshire racecourse, home of the St Leger.
annotation.definitionFit: Doncaster is a major English horse-racing course.

annotation.surface: A fight against the royal family.
annotation.walkthrough: AGIN is the rustic form of against, common in crosswords.
annotation.definitionFit: Agincourt was Henry V's victory over the French in 1415.

annotation.surface: Evidence that backs up a case.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface reads as one idea, backing up evidence, but the definition is only the last word.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: evidence strong enough to settle a question.

entries.clue: Bust is cut for a cross (9)

indicatorNotes.Bust: broken, so the letters that follow are scrambled

annotation.surface: A bust carved for a crucifix, or a sculpture chiselled into a cross.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Bust' looks like a statue and 'cross' like a shape; one scrambles, the other means bad-tempered.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: cross in the sense of irritable and quarrelsome.

entries.clue: Simpson held by record company as an icon (5)

indicatorNotes.held by: the record company holds the Simpson inside it

annotation.surface: A Simpson signed to a record label as a star.
annotation.walkthrough: Simpson suggests Homer or Bart; it is O.J.
annotation.definitionFit: An emoji is a small digital icon used in messages.

blocks.note: to earn a crust is to earn a living
an ace is a one on dice or cards

annotation.surface: A single living shellfish.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Living' looks like alive; it is a livelihood, as in earning a crust.
annotation.definitionFit: Crustacea are the class of shellfish that includes crabs and lobsters.

entries.clue: Piece of music as farewell after prison (7)

indicatorNotes.after: the farewell comes after the prison

annotation.surface: A song of goodbye played for someone leaving jail.
annotation.walkthrough: CAN is American slang for prison.
annotation.definitionFit: Definition by category: a work for voices and instruments, such as Bach wrote weekly for church.

entries.clue: Sam is one, and mostly dirty (7)

indicatorNotes.mostly: most of the word, losing its last letter

annotation.surface: A man called Sam who is, for the most part, filthy.
annotation.walkthrough: Uncle Sam personifies the United States.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym, covering both physical grime and ritual impurity.

entries.clue: A crossing made by Drake’s ship once (7)

blocks.note: a British pedestrian crossing with push-button lights

annotation.surface: A sea voyage made in Francis Drake's old ship.
annotation.walkthrough: The crossing sounds like a sea voyage; a pelican crossing is a UK road crossing with lights.
annotation.definitionFit: Drake's Golden Hind set out as the Pelican; the pelican crossing is a street crossing.

blocks.note: a verb: to cram or squash in
an old or Irish and Scottish word for a linen cupboard

annotation.surface: Things kept in a cupboard.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Stuff' is a verb, to cram, not the noun for things.
annotation.definitionFit: Press means stuff or cram, and in Scotland and Ireland a press is a cupboard.

entries.clue: How Pierre will give you an opinion (7)

blocks.note: Pierre signals a French speaker, so we want the French word for how

annotation.surface: A Frenchman explaining how he will tell you what he thinks.
annotation.walkthrough: Pierre stands for any French speaker, so 'How, Pierre' is the French word.
annotation.definitionFit: Two senses: the French word for how, and the English noun for a remark voicing a view.

blocks.note: the surface wants the running race; the setter means the Maltese cross and the George Cross

annotation.surface: A cross-country run.
annotation.walkthrough: Cross-country sounds like running; Malta is the country of the Maltese cross, and was awarded the George Cross.
annotation.definitionFit: Malta gives its name to the Maltese cross and carries the George Cross on its flag.

annotation.surface: Timing a journey to catch a train.
annotation.walkthrough: The train is not a railway train but a retinue, like a bride's train of attendants.
annotation.definitionFit: A less common sense of train: the retinue of attendants following an important person.

annotation.surface: A Latin title given to a German board game.
annotation.walkthrough: The 'German' qualifies the name, OTTO, not the game.
annotation.definitionFit: Lotto is a game of chance, like bingo.

entries.clue: Zip was fastened, many an alteration to it (5,5,5)

indicatorNotes.an alteration to it: the words before it are altered, their letters rearranged

annotation.surface: A zip done up, but needing plenty of repairs.
annotation.walkthrough: The zip sounds like a fastener; it is zip meaning nothing. Sweet Fanny Adams is British slang for nothing at all.
annotation.definitionFit: Sweet Fanny Adams, or sweet FA, means nothing whatsoever, just as zip does.
